articles.title: 'Ek ball karane do, please' - From boxing rings to 147 first-class wickets: Bishworjit Konthoujam’s unlikely journey began with one request
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: When North East Zone pacer Bishworjit Konthoujam came into the attack during the Duleep Trophy quarterfinal against East Zone, all eyes wer.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: When North East Zone pacer Bishworjit Konthoujam came into the attack during the Duleep Trophy quarterfinal against East Zone, all eyes were on the batter facing him - 15-year-old batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.The expectations were clear. Boundaries. Big hits. Perhaps even a few towering sixes.And Sooryavanshi did exactly what many expected from him. After playing out his first two balls, the young batter hit the Manipur pacer for two boundaries in a row. He had taken Konthoujam on.But the 30-year-old had the last laugh.Soon after being hit for the two fours, Konthoujam dismissed Sooryavanshi, ending the young star's stay at the crease. The pacer leapt into the air in celebration before receiving high-fives from his teammates.For many watching, it was just another wicket. For Bishworjit, however, the moment was a reminder of how far he had travelled. Because before he began troubling batters with a cricket ball, he was busy throwing punches in a boxing ring.The accidental cricketerBefore picking up a leather ball, Bishworjit Konthoujam wore boxing gloves. Jab. Cross. Hook. Uppercut.Boxing was his first love. He won medals at school and state-level competitions. He trained hard and dreamed of making a career in the sport.But there was another game he enjoyed - cricket.Like many youngsters in India, Bishworjit loved the game. However, he played only for fun. Whenever he found a group of children playing cricket in his village, he wanted to join them.Walking through the streets of Patsoi Part IV, his residence in Manipur, if he saw youngsters playing cricket, he would often stop and ask: “Ek ball karane do, please” - let me bowl just one ball.He played cricket whenever he had time away from his boxing training.“Cricket was always my second love after boxing. But I never imagined that one day I would leave boxing and become a cricketer,” Bishworjit told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.“I give a lot of credit to Ronel sir. Whatever I am today is because of him. He saw something in me and pushed me towards cricket. Leaving boxing wasn't easy at all,” he said.One conversation changed everythingLeishangthem Ronel Singh, secretary of the Manipur Cricket Association, first noticed Bishworjit while he was bowling with a tennis ball during a local game. The young boxer had never received formal cricket coaching, but his bowling caught Ronel's attention.He had pace. He could move the ball. And he had a natural bowling action.Ronel was impressed and suggested that Bishworjit should seriously consider cricket. Bishworjit took his time before making the decision. Then he decided to give the sport a chance. He put his boxing gloves aside and picked up a leather ball.That was the beginning of a journey that would eventually take him from local grounds in Manipur to the Ranji Trophy and Duleep Trophy.“I had never played proper cricket with a leather ball, so it was very difficult in the beginning,” Bishworjit said.“Boxing taught me many things. It taught me how to fight, how to come back and how to get up after falling down. I needed all those things in cricket as well. Leather-ball cricket was completely new to me, but slowly cricket became everything for me.”Learning the art of fast bowlingSwitching from tennis-ball cricket to leather-ball cricket was not easy. The grip was different. The release was different. The ball behaved differently.Bishworjit had to learn everything from the beginning. But his years in boxing had made him physically strong and mentally tough. He quickly adapted to the demands of fast bowling.After playing in local tournaments, Bishworjit began making a name for himself in Manipur. He represented the state at the U-23 level before getting the big break he had been waiting for.He made his first-class debut for Manipur against Sikkim in 2018.There was no looking back after that.Manipur’s wicket machineBishworjit made an immediate impact in the 2018-19 Ranji Trophy season. He finished as Manipur's highest wicket-taker, picking up 30 wickets in just eight matches. He was also among the top 10 wicket-takers in the country that season.Since then, he has become one of the most successful cricketers from the state.The right-arm medium pacer has played 48 first-class matches, 49 List A games and 46 T20 matches. He has taken 147 wickets in first-class cricket, including three five-wicket hauls. He also has 66 List A and 46 T20 wickets to his name.He was also Manipur's leading wicket-taker in the 2018-19 Vijay Hazare Trophy.In the 2019-20 Vijay Hazare Trophy, he produced a memorable seven-wicket haul, including a hat-trick, against Nagaland.Bishworjit has also taken five-wicket hauls against Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram in the Ranji Trophy.He became the first fast bowler from the North East Zone to take more than 100 first-class wickets and the second player from the region overall to reach the mark. He was also the first player from the North East to take more than 50 wickets in List A cricket.Today, Bishworjit is the leading wicket-taker from the North East Zone across all three formats.His journey also took him beyond India when he became the first cricketer from Manipur to play for an English club, Tynemouth Cricket Club.Bowling on slopes and in the rainBishworjit's journey was far from easy. Before Manipur became a full member of the BCCI and entered India's major domestic tournaments, the state had limited cricket facilities.For a fast bowler, finding a proper place to train was a major challenge.Manipur also receives heavy rainfall for several months every year, making regular outdoor practice difficult.Bishworjit and other young cricketers had to find their own ways to train.“We did not have many facilities before 2018. It rains heavily in Manipur from June to September, so practising was very difficult,” he said.“Sometimes we practised on slopes because we felt running uphill could help us build strength and generate more pace. After the rain, we would put sand on wet areas to make the surface usable and then start bowling again.”The situation, he says, has changed significantly now.The BCCI has helped improve cricket infrastructure in the state, with players now having access to better training facilities.“Things have changed a lot. The BCCI has done a great job for cricket in Manipur and given us much better facilities,” he said.“Life has become much easier for young cricketers now. They have facilities that we did not have when we started.”The meeting with Vaibhav SooryavanshiNorth East Zone lost the Duleep Trophy quarterfinal, but Bishworjit still wanted to meet Sooryavanshi after the match.The 30-year-old walked towards the East Zone dressing room and met the teenager. They shared a smile and shook hands.Bishworjit had watched Sooryavanshi closely during his rise in the IPL, the Under-19 World Cup and international cricket.“He is a very nice boy and a special talent. I have watched him in the IPL, the Under-19 World Cup and for India. The way he hits the ball is incredible,” Bishworjit said.“But I also told him that red-ball cricket requires patience. You have to give yourself some time at the crease.”Sooryavanshi had shown his attacking style by hitting Bishworjit for two boundaries before the pacer got his wicket.For the Manipur bowler, it was a small example of the difference between white-ball and red-ball cricket.“He had a lot of time to bat. That is the difference between red-ball and white-ball cricket,” Bishworjit said.“In red-ball cricket, patience is very important. You cannot play every ball the way you do in white-ball cricket. We spoke about cricket and exchanged a few thoughts,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Is this from the Pakistani willow?’ ‘It’s never hit a ball’: Cricket fans roast Babar Azam after he gifts signed bat to King Charles
articles.summary: Babar Azam faced a barrage of online mockery after gifting a signed bat to King Charles.
articles.body:
Babar Azam presented King Charles III with a Pakistan -squad-signed bat during the team's visit to Clarence House.

Fans quickly mocked the gesture, questioning whether the bat had ever been used.

Pakistan already lost the England Test series 2-0, making the third Test at Edgbaston a dead rubber.

Pakistan tour in crisis as Babar gifts signed bat to King Charles

With Pakistan losing both the first two tests by innings and 103 runs at Headingley and 194 runs at Lord's respectively, their England tour has become a crisis as the series is now all but wrapped up 2-0 in favour of England.

This forced a complete overhaul of the team where seven players have been released , which includes Mohammad Rizwan and Salman Ali Agha along with the head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and the bowling coach Umar Gul.

Amidst all the chaos, Babar and the rest of the Pakistan team met with King Charles III on September 2 at Clarence House. Babar gifted the king a bat signed by his teammates. The gesture, however, quickly became a social media joke.

Fans turn Babar's King Charles gesture into a roast

One fan commented : "Apparently it's never hit a ball. It was used in the last 2 tests."

Another suggested King Charles inquire if it had been made using Pakistani willow, saying, "He is asking, is this from the Pakistani willow? Babar be like yes yes from all Pakistani players bruhhhh."

Similarly, yet another mocked Babar's understanding of bat construction: "Does babar azam know bats are made of English willow, not 'Pakistan willow'?"

Further on, the comments went. One fan asked : "I wonder if the dropped players signed this bat."

Even Iceland Cricket added into the fun: "You can bet he didn't know who most of the players were, because nobody else does."

The jokes continued with another fan speculating , "They offered him the job of bowling coach as well."

The bat itself received most of the mockery after the Pakistan batters' failures in the first two Test matches, and perhaps due to the poor timing of such an award, with the team still reeling from its second loss of the series.

Bat joke on Babar reflects Pakistan cricket's bigger problem

The bat jokes are harmless jibes, but they speak volumes about the frustration with Pakistani cricket.

Signed bat is a common courtesy. However, with back-to-back losses, wholesale team changes, and a coach shuffle, the circumstances made it easy for the gift of the bat to be ridiculed.

What really matters is not whether or not the bat has ever hit the ball, but that Pakistan starts performing to their potential.

articles.body:
Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) Chairman Mohsin Naqvi has defended the major changes made to Pakistan's Test squad during the ongoing England series, saying the decisions were "essential". Pakistan made sweeping changes before the third and final Test against England, scheduled to begin on September 9. The new players include Arafat Minhas, Mohammad Imran Jnr, Saad Baig, Mohammad Imran Randhawa and Razaullah. articles.title: England v Australia Ashes ticket price increase 'really poor' - Michael Vaughan
articles.summary: Former England captain Michael Vaughan is critical of a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston.
articles.body:
Former England captain Michael Vaughan has called a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston "really poor".

The Birmingham ground will host the third Test of the best-of-five series between England and Australia next summer, with ticket prices in the Hollies Stand - which holds almost 6,000 spectators - costing £165, up from £115 in 2023.

Elsewhere in the stadium, members can purchase tickets for £92, but the cheapest adult tickets across the first three days are £115, with every ticket carrying a £2.50 booking fee.

"This is really poor," Vaughan posted on social media in response to the news.

Following the 2023 series, which ended in a 2-2 draw after Australia won the first two Tests (at Edgbaston and Lord's), the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) said "every day sold out in advance, with total attendance topping 545,000".

An Edgbaston Stadium spokesperson said: "Our prices for the 2027 Ashes Test are broadly in line with other host venues and major British sporting events such as Wimbledon and the Formula One at Silverstone.

"Our entry level ticket prices roughly match inflation compared to the last time Australia visited Edgbaston in 2023 - but like the rest of the country, we're battling increased costs and trying to manage these wherever we can."

Despite Warwickshire's Edgbaston stadium being at a reduced capacity because of the construction of an on-site hotel, tickets for next week's third Test between England and Pakistan, which range between £57.50-£87.50 for adults, have not sold out.

The ticket ballot for the 2027 Ashes opened on Wednesday, with prices more expensive at Lord's and the Oval in London, with the best tickets at £190 and £185.

England, who lost 4-1 in Australia last winter, begin their quest to regain the Ashes at Trent Bridge in Nottingham on 18 June.

The second Ashes Test at Lord's begins on 30 June and the third at Edgbaston on 8 July.

The Utilita Bowl in Southampton will become the 10th UK ground to host a men's Ashes Test when the fourth Test gets under way on 21 July, with the series concluding at the Kia Oval from 29 July.

BBC Sport has contacted the ECB and all the Test venues for comment.

Ticket prices for sporting events have been an ongoing point of contention for fans.

A crowd of 13,623 were at Birmingham's 23,000-capacity Alexander Stadium to watch Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt win the women's 100m at the European Athletics Championships last month.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with Category A tickets for the home straight costing £150.

For the men's 100m final those same seats cost £110, again with no concessions for juniors.

In April, Ryder Cup organisers defended ticket prices for next year's centenary golf event between Europe and the United States in Ireland.

Daily general admission tickets for the three tournament days on 17-19 September at Adare Manor in County Limerick will cost 499 euros (£434), compared with up to 260 euros in Italy in 2023.

articles.body: Pakistan’s cricket team was caught up in more controversy after players who had been dropped from the Test squad were told to attend a meeting with King Charles III at Clarence House.According to a report from The Telegraph, the Pakistan Cricket Board reportedly wanted to avoid an awkwardly small turnout after making major changes to the touring squad. One other dropped player even refused to attend in protest.Dropped players still attend royal meetingSeven players and several coaches were removed from the touring group following Pakistan’s defeats to England at Lord’s and Headingley. Despite being dropped, players were reportedly instructed to attend the royal engagement.Ali Usman, Aamir Jamal, Khurram Shahzad and Muhammad Awais Zafar attended the meeting, although players had reportedly preferred to stay away because of the turmoil within the team.King Charles spoke with the players and officials and offered encouragement during a difficult tour. Pakistan captain Babar Azam presented him with a signed bat, while PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi also gave the King a gift.Naqvi described the meeting as positive and said the King praised Pakistan’s contribution to peace.Turmoil continues around Pakistan teamThe royal meeting came during a major shake-up in Pakistan cricket. The team faced further controversy at Lord’s when it threatened not to return after lunch if an interview with the sons of former captain and prime minister Imran Khan was broadcast.The interview aired, but Pakistan returned to the field before losing the match. The defeat was followed by the removal of seven players and coaches, while head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed was sacked.New Zealander Mike Hesson has since been brought in to lead the team for the remainder of the series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Auqib Nabi fails to impress, goes wicketless on day one of County debut
articles.summary: Cricket News: Indian cricketers had a mixed first day in the latest round of the County Championship on Wednesday, with Yuzvendra Chahal picking up a wicket for Nor.
articles.body: Indian cricketers had a mixed first day in the latest round of the County Championship on Wednesday, with Yuzvendra Chahal picking up a wicket for Northamptonshire, Mayank Agarwal remaining unbeaten for Durham, and Surrey duo Auqib Nabi and Rahul Chahar going wicketless.Several Indian players are featuring across Division One and Division Two of this year's County Championship.Auqib Nabi, Rahul Chahar go wicketless for SurreySurrey bowlers Auqib Nabi and Rahul Chahar could not pick up a wicket on the opening day of their Division One match against Yorkshire.Pacer Auqib bowled 11 overs, conceded 25 runs and remained wicketless. Leg-spinner Rahul Chahar bowled only two overs on a rain-affected day.Yorkshire ended Day 1 on 133/7 after 59.5 overs.India spinner Kuldeep Yadav, playing for Yorkshire, came in at No. 9 and was unbeaten on 6 at stumps.Chahal strikes, Agarwal unbeaten for DurhamIn the Division Two match between Durham and Northamptonshire, Yuzvendra Chahal dismissed Durham captain Alex Lees to give Northamptonshire an important breakthrough.For Durham, opener Mayank Agarwal was unbeaten on 25 at the close of play.Durham finished Day 1 on 129/3 after 30.5 overs.Manav Suthar, Sai Kishore await Day 2 actionIndia left-arm spinner Manav Suthar, who is part of Warwickshire's squad in their Division One match against Hampshire, did not get a chance to bat on the opening day.Warwickshire ended the day on 141/1 after 41 overs.Sai Kishore was also not involved on Day 1 as Gloucestershire finished on 62/5 after 31 overs against Derbyshire in Division One.Kishore is expected to come into the game with both bat and ball on Day 2.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: English cricketer runs 100km from Lord’s Cricket Ground in unique Guinness World record attempt
articles.summary: Cricket News: English club cricketer and endurance athlete Sam Bodoano has completed an extraordinary 62-mile (100km) run from Lord’s Cricket Ground in London to Va.
articles.body: English club cricketer and endurance athlete Sam Bodoano has completed an extraordinary 62-mile (100km) run from Lord’s Cricket Ground in London to Valley End Cricket Club in Woking, Surrey, in an attempt to set a Guinness World Record for the longest run-up before bowling a cricket ball.Bodoano, 22, from Worplesdon near Guildford, Surrey, began his run at Lord’s on Saturday and completed the gruelling journey around 14 hours later at Valley End Cricket Club on Sunday. His challenge culminated in him bowling the opening delivery of an 11-a-side match to his father.Bodoano completes gruelling run in full cricket whitesTo meet the requirements for the record attempt, Bodoano had to complete the entire 100km journey in full cricket whites while carrying a cricket ball. He then had to take part in a cricket match and deliver the opening ball. While Bodoano has completed the challenge and believes he has surpassed the existing mark, Guinness World Records has not yet officially recognised the achievement. The organisation's evidence review and verification process is still under way.A Guinness World Records spokesperson said the application would need to go through the formal evidence review process before the record could be officially confirmed. The review can take around two weeks, depending on the evidence submitted.If confirmed, Bodoano's run-up would comfortably surpass the previous men's record of 15 miles. The current holder of the record for the longest bowling run-up (male) is Tom Dunn, who ran 15 miles (24km) from Bethnal Green, in east London, to Wandsworth Common, in south London, in August 2024.100km challenge raises almost £6,000 for charityDespite the physical demands of the challenge, Bodoano completed the run for a charitable cause, raising almost £6,000 (Rs 7,64,513) for The Ruth Strauss Foundation, a cancer charity founded by former England captain Sir Andrew Strauss."I'm very tired, I lost a lot of sleep, but it was all for an amazing cause," Bodoano said.An experienced endurance athlete, Bodoano has previously competed in the England Hockey Men's Premier League, completed the London Marathon and Ironman Wales, and finished third in a 112-mile backyard ultra-marathon. He also works as a running coach and content creator.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: VVS Laxman to step in as Team India head coach for Asian Games 2026 in Gautam Gambhir’s absence
articles.summary: Cricket News: Former India batter and Director of Cricket at the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence, VVS Laxman, is set to travel with the Indian men’s team to Japan and w.
articles.body: Former India batter and Director of Cricket at the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence, VVS Laxman, is set to travel with the Indian men’s team to Japan and will take charge as head coach in the absence of Gautam Gambhir for the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya later this month.Gautam Gambhir will remain with the senior side for India’s home ODI series against the West Indies. The first ODI is scheduled to be played on September 27.Laxman will be assisted by former India spinner Sunil Joshi, Hrishikesh Kanitkar and Subhadeep Ghosh, according to the list of coaches released by the Sports Ministry. The development was earlier reported by TimesofIndia.com in July.Laxman has previous Asian Games experience, having coached the Indian men’s team at the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, where India won the gold medal.India to defend Men’s and Women’s Asian Games cricket titlesThe cricket competition at the Asian Games will begin on September 24, with India scheduled to play its opening men’s match on September 28. India will defend its men’s T20 title under captain Shreyas Iyer, with teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi also part of the squad. The men’s team will face the second-placed side from Group A, which comprises Afghanistan, Japan and Nepal.The Indian women’s team will also enter the tournament as defending champions and will be led by Harmanpreet Kaur. The women’s side will enter the competition at the quarterfinal stage and face hosts Japan. Amol Muzumdar will continue as the head coach of the women’s team, with bowling coach Aavishkar Salvi and fielding coach Munish Bali completing his support staff.Indian cricket teams for Asian Games 2026Indian men’s team: Shreyas Iyer (captain), Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson, Ishan Kishan, Shivam Dube, Tilak Varma, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Axar Patel, Washington Sundar, Varun Chakravarthy, Ravi Bishnoi, Jasprit Bumrah, Harshit Rana, Arshdeep Singh, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.Indian women’s team: Harmanpreet Kaur (captain), Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma, Pratika Rawal, Deepti Sharma, Richa Ghosh, Gunalan Kamalini, Bharti Fulmali, Sree Charani, Renuka Thakur, Kranti Gaud, Arundhati Reddy, Shreyanka Patil, Radha Yadav, Nandani Sharma.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘It’s only a frikkin game’: Wasim Akram recalls helping Irfan Pathan before his anti-Pakistan posts
articles.summary: Cricket News: Pakistan great Wasim Akram has urged fans on both sides of the India-Pakistan divide to stop carrying the emotions of past conflicts into cricket, ins.
articles.body: Pakistan great Wasim Akram has urged fans on both sides of the India-Pakistan divide to stop carrying the emotions of past conflicts into cricket, insisting that one of the sport’s fiercest rivalries should ultimately be treated as nothing more than a game.Akram, while speaking on the 1 Mint podcast, also reflected on his long-standing association with former India all-rounder Irfan Pathan, recalling how the young left-armer was a huge fan of his when the two first met in Australia. Akram said he gave Pathan a few tips early in his career, but joked that his former admirer now regularly posts comments against Pakistan on social media.“It’s a different thing that he keeps tweeting some or the other thing against Pakistan. But our fans are ready too. They don’t have the tendency to ignore either. They just have to reply,” Akram said.The comments came while Akram was discussing the extraordinary attention and emotion surrounding India-Pakistan matches, which have increasingly become a battleground on social media as much as they are contests on the cricket field.‘It’s only a frikkin game’Akram, who played in some of the most memorable India-Pakistan contests of his era, believes fans should not allow sporting results to become an extension of historical and political tensions.“People have too much time. Why can’t they understand? It’s only a frikkin game. At the end of the day, it’s just a match. Somebody has to win, somebody has to lose. And move on to the next one,” he said.“But no, what happened many moons ago still lingers. Revenge and all is so 1970. It’s the classic ‘an empty mind is a devil’s workshop’ thought process,” he added.Akram's message comes at a time when every India-Pakistan encounter generates enormous discussion online, with supporters often carrying the rivalry well beyond the boundaries of the cricket field.For the former Pakistan captain, however, the basic principle remains simple: one side wins, the other loses, and both move on.When Akram helped a young Irfan PathanAkram also recalled his first interaction with Pathan, who grew up watching Pakistan's legendary left-arm fast bowlers and was frequently compared with Akram after bursting onto the international scene.“Irfan met me in 2004 on his first tour to Australia; I was commentating. He was a big fan. Grew up watching us. I gave him a few tips here and there, but he did well early on in his career,” Akram said.Pathan's bowling action bore similarities to Akram's, and the Pakistani great explained that his advice was less about changing the young bowler's technique and more about helping him understand the tactical aspects of fast bowling.“His action was similar to mine from the very beginning. But when players ask you about something, what you tell them is mostly about the mindset. Action and all is fine, because at that stage, you have reached that level where you’re representing the country,” he said.“Things like wrist position and how to suss out a batsman. When to use variations, when not to. So yeah, it was good fun. Irfan is a good boy; he still keeps meeting me.”Pathan went on to become one of India's most effective left-arm fast bowlers of the 2000s. His ability to swing the new ball and generate movement made comparisons with Akram inevitable, while his versatility eventually turned him into an important all-rounder.Pathan and his Pakistan rivalryPathan also developed a formidable record against Pakistan, taking 67 wickets in 36 internationals — 27 in Tests, 34 in ODIs and six in T20Is.One of his most memorable performances came in Karachi in 2006, when he became only the second Indian to take a Test hat-trick, removing Salman Butt, Younis Khan and Mohammad Yousuf in the first over of the innings.Since retirement, Pathan has remained one of the most outspoken former Indian cricketers on social media and television. He has occasionally taken aim at Pakistan and its cricketers, including during the aftermath of high-profile India-Pakistan encounters.Akram, however, appeared to take the banter in his stride. While acknowledging Pathan's occasional anti-Pakistan posts, he also pointed out that fans on both sides are equally unwilling to let such comments pass.But the former Pakistan captain wants the line between sporting competition and everything beyond it to remain clear.“Somebody has to win, somebody has to lose. And move on to the next one,” Akram said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘India lost to Ireland. Has cricket ended?’: Mohsin Naqvi hits back at critics, defends Pakistan cricket shake-up
articles.summary: Cricket News: Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) chairman Mohsin Naqvi has hit back at the growing criticism of Pakistan cricket, questioning whether a few defeats should.
articles.body: Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) chairman Mohsin Naqvi has hit back at the growing criticism of Pakistan cricket, questioning whether a few defeats should be enough to declare the sport in the country “finished” while pointing to India’s recent T20I loss to Ireland as an example of how even top sides can suffer unexpected setbacks.Speaking to the media in London, Naqvi defended the PCB’s controversial decisions during Pakistan’s disastrous Test tour of England and insisted that the team’s recent struggles should be viewed in the wider context of its improving white-ball record.“Let me ask you one thing: South Africa lost to Namibia, and India lost to Ireland. Has cricket ended there as well?” Naqvi said.The PCB chief's reference to India came as he sought to push back against those who have questioned Pakistan's direction following back-to-back heavy defeats in the Test series against England.“Yes, one thing is important: whoever we need here, we will definitely bring in. If someone is not clicking or not performing, then what can we do? Every match and every series is important for us,” he added.‘Our cricket is finished?’Pakistan suffered an innings-and-103-run defeat in the opening Test before losing the second match at Lord’s by 194 runs. The results handed England an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series and triggered a major overhaul of the touring squad.The PCB released seven players — Mohammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman, Aamir Jamal, Muhammad Awais Zafar and Khurram Shahzad — ahead of the Birmingham Test, while bringing in several younger players.Naqvi defended the sweeping changes and rejected claims that Pakistan cricket had reached its lowest point.“You used to be ranked eighth in ODIs, which has now gone up to fifth. You have had six ODI series, out of which you have won four, but still, our cricket is finished?” he said.“Our success rate has gone up from 24 per cent to 73 per cent, and I'm not talking about just one or the other specific match, but still, our cricket is finished?”Pakistan currently sit fifth in the ODI rankings and sixth in T20Is, according to Naqvi, who argued that rebuilding a struggling side could not happen overnight.“It is not possible to take a team from number nine to number one in three or six months. There is a long way to go,” he said.Naqvi takes aim at criticsNaqvi was particularly scathing about those who have criticised the PCB and its handling of the team, saying he was not opposed to criticism but questioning the credentials of some of his detractors.“I have never been afraid of criticism, and I never will be,” he said.“Those players who have never achieved anything in their lives, when they talk along these lines, that's unreasonable.”He said he regularly sought opinions from former cricketers and would accept criticism when it came from respected figures.“If a great player like Wasim Akram spoke, I would take it seriously,” Naqvi said, while insisting that some critics were more interested in targeting him personally than addressing Pakistan cricket's problems.At the same time, Naqvi acknowledged that the PCB had made mistakes, particularly in selection, and said he was willing to take responsibility.“Sometimes there are mistakes made in selection as well. I am answerable for that, and we need to work on it,” he said.The board's selection decisions have come under further scrutiny after it issued notices to selection committee members Aaqib Javed, Misbah-ul-Haq and Asad Shafiq, seeking explanations over the recommendations of Rizwan and Imam.Misbah subsequently decided to resign from the selection committee.Despite the turmoil, Naqvi insisted that changes were necessary if players were not delivering and that he would not allow the team to be demoralised.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
